title: Photosynthesis: Conversion of Light into Chemical Energy
summary: This lesson explores photosynthesis, the biological process used by photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms to convert light energy into chemical energy. It covers both oxygenic and anoxygenic photosynthesis, light-dependent reactions, and the Calvin cycle.

sections.text: Scene: A diagram showing a schematic of photosynthesis in plants, illustrating how carbohydrates are produced and stored. A composite image displays the global distribution of photosynthesis, with dark red and blue-green indicating high photosynthetic activity in the ocean and on land. I wonder...?: What do photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms convert light energy into? Answer: They convert light energy into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism.

Scene: A microscopic view showing purple bacteria utilizing bacteriochlorophyll to split hydrogen sulfide. Archaea are shown using retinal and microbial rhodopsin derivatives to absorb green light and produce a proton gradient across the cell membrane. I wonder...?: What does anoxygenic photosynthesis release instead of oxygen? Answer: It releases sulfur when using hydrogen sulfide as a reductant.
Light-Dependent Reactions and the Calvin Cycle

Scene: Chloroplasts in leaf cells containing chlorophylls that absorb red and blue spectra of light while reflecting green. A sequence depicts atmospheric carbon dioxide being incorporated into organic compounds like ribulose bisphosphate using ATP and NADPH. I wonder...?: What sequence of light-independent reactions synthesizes sugars in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria? Answer: The Calvin cycle.

learning_objectives: Define photosynthesis and distinguish between oxygenic and anoxygenic photosynthesis.
Describe the role of light-dependent reactions and pigments like chlorophyll.
Explain how the Calvin cycle synthesizes sugars using ATP and NADPH.

vocabulary.definition: A system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms convert light energy into chemical energy.
Organisms that are able to synthesize food directly from carbon dioxide and water using energy from light.
A sequence of light-independent reactions where atmospheric carbon dioxide is incorporated into already existing organic compounds to form carbohydrates.
